title: How to free Mert in The Blood of Dawnwalker
author: Sean Martin
text:
Finding a way to free Mert in Blood of Dawnwalker 's Under Watchful Eyes quest took me a while to work out. At first, I slaughtered the entire fort, but after such a slog of a fight I realised there must be a better way to do it—turns out there is. You can take a sneakier route at nighttime which drastically reduces the number of soldiers you have to kill.
In my video runthrough of it below, I also show how to reduce the number of fights even further with some tactically-employed Voracious Bites. Here's how to free Mert without murdering the fort.
How to free Mert without killing everyone in Stoneward Post
There's an obvious approach to freeing Mert in Under Watchful Eyes, and that's killing every soldier in the fort, but this is understandably quite tricky. There is a sneakier route you can take via a back door instead which will really cut down the number of goons you've got to put down.
You can avoid the two-on-one fight in Friedo's office by following my exact route in the video above. To do it, you need to purchase the Shadow Dweller and Dimension Reach upgrades in the Vampirism tree so you can take a shortcut up to the battlements. These are generally very handy upgrades, though, as they buff Shadow Reach distance and reduce stamina used in Plane Walking.
Steal the prison keys from Friedo's office Rebel Wolves Return at night to the backdoor of Stoneward Post Rebel Wolves Unlock the door with the keys you stole for an easy way in and out Rebel Wolves If you don't, you'll have to fight a bunch of enemies in the upper courtyard outside Mert's office, Friedo and the miniboss in his office, and the prison guard by the cells. Even without the Shadow Step skip, you're still fighting far fewer soldiers than if you'd taken on the whole fort. These are the steps you need to take if you have the upgrades.
After you've first spoken to Mert, go back up to Friedo's office and steal the Prison Keyring hanging on rightside shelves—he should be facing the opposite way, so just press Ctrl to sneak and yoink them. If you didn't do this the first time, return to the fort and grab them.
Leave the fort and do other activities until moonrise (nighttime).
Go around the back of the fort and use the Prison Keyring to unlock the back door.
Head inside, use Shadow Step and Planewalking to reach the top of the tower to your right, and walk along the battlements until you're above Friedo's office.
Get to a spot where you can Voracious Bite him to put him to sleep (as shown in the video)
Take everything of value in the chests and head downstairs.
Voracious Bite the guard by the prison cells to put him to sleep.
Free Mert.
When you head back upstairs, you'll have to fight the miniboss, Rayko the Incorruptible, and then three soldiers outside and a dog afterwards.
You can also take out one of the outside soldiers with a Voracious Bite before any of the others get to you (also shown in the video). After they're dealt with, make sure you're above one health segment , then exit the back door with Mert. He'll thank you and ask where to go, and you can send him to the Almshouse in Svartrau.
This is one of those hunger moments, so if you're below one health bar, I'm pretty sure you'd be forced to feed on Mert instead, which would be a poor reward for all your hard work. It's worth noting that whether you killed the soldiers at the mill during The Firebrand will also have an impact on Renna and Mert's potentially happy ending.

title: How to beat the Ravenous Bear and complete Into the Den in The Blood of Dawnwalker
author: Sean Martin
text:
Fighting the Ravenous Bear is an early combat challenge in Blood of Dawnwalker 's prologue, but mainly because you don't have many skills or decent equipment yet, which turns the fight into a slog. After you do defeat it, you'll also have to track down a treasure as part of the Into the Den quest. I'll run through how to do both below.
How to beat the Ravenous Bear in Blood of Dawnwalker
The Ravenous Bear is the most challenging early boss you can encounter near Laslea. Here are some tips to beat it, plus a video of me fighting the bear above so you can see the strategy in action:
Get a better sword : The fight will be over faster if you get a decent weapon. I recommend heading across to the other side of the lake, looking for the big tree with the wolves, and completing the Deep Down quest. This will get you the Undead Warrior's Sword, which is a nice upgrade over what you had.
Parry its regular attacks, but dodge to the side of its red unblockable ones : Parrying is better in this fight because you're less likely to run out stamina (which dodging consumes), so you can keep attacking. When the bear attacks with a red skull, dodge to the side, rather than away. This will give you a window to deal more damage, too.
Time your Perfect Parries when the shield turns orange: This tripped me up quite a bit at first since I was trying to time parries based on the directional attack indicator, but it's much better to time your parries based on when the shield turns from yellow to orange. This is far more consistent.
Watch your stamina : If you start to run low on stamina, back off, and try to Perfect Parry any jumping attacks the bear makes at you while your stamina recovers a bit.
With all that, you should be able to defeat the bear, and then check the mangled corpse behind it to start the Into the Den quest.
How to complete Into the Den in Blood of Dawnwalker
You can find the stone marked with X in the logging camp in the north of the valley Rebel Wolves Look for the only small hut with a door in the camp Rebel Wolves Head inside to find the X and the treasure Rebel Wolves Reading the Tattered Letter you find on the corpse will begin Into the Den, giving you a search area to the northwest where you need to look for the stash mentioned in the note. Specifically, you're looking for a "flat stone marked with an X".
You can find this inside in the ramshackle hut with the door on the west side of the search area —it's the only structure with a door, so it's hard to miss. If still confused, follow the nearby shrine west along the road and you'll spot the hut to your left as you pass.
Loot the treasure (which will take one time cycle) to get the very snazzy-looking Artisan's Tunic, the extremely good Rebel's Falchion shortsword, plus a handy note about where to sell any silver you might find later in the game, a substance strictly prohibited by the vamps for obvious reasons.

title: How to sell silver in The Blood of Dawnwalker
author: Andrea Shearon
text:
I had no trouble finding vendors to offload Coen's endless supply of low-value pilfered junk in Blood of Dawnwalker , but it took a few days to figure out how to sell silver . It makes sense that silver is considered contraband under vampire rule, so you have to find the right vendor to foist it on and complete a quick quest before adventuring south.
Where can you sell silver in Blood of Dawnwalker?
(Image credit: Rebel Wolves) You can sell silver in Svartrau City to the aptly named Silver Trader, but before you leave Coen's home in Laslea Glen, complete the Into the Den quest. It doesn't take long to slay the ravenous bear, and you need the intel uncovered by investigating what remains of its dinner.
Any item with a white chalice icon is silver contraband
Complete Into the Den, a quest that begins east of the Northern Foothill
Head south to Svatrau City and speak with the Silver Trader
Tell him you know he's dealing in silver, and he'll agree to trade
In the name of RPG science, I tried heading to Svartrau immediately and skipping Into the Den, but the Silver Trader just tells Coen to get lost. You've gotta kill the bear, sorry.
A note at the end of the quest points Coen to Svartrau's Neustadt District. The city is further away in south-central Vale Sangora, but as long as you've completed Into the Den, you can visit as early or as late as you want. The map populates with new merchant icons and quest icons when you're close—the Silver Trader is in the southwest corner.
When he plays coy about Coen's visit, tell the Silver Trader you know what he's up to, and he'll agree to buy your silver contraband. It sells for way more than all of those pickles and chunks of raw meat in Coen's pockets. Well worth the bear fight, if you ask me.

title: CD Projekt mystery games update: Yes, they're still happening, and no, not any time soon
author: Andy Chalk
text:
CD Projekt has a lot going on these days: The Witcher 4 , Cyberpunk 2 , a new Witcher 3 expansion and remaster , a remake of the original Witcher , probably some other stuff I've either forgotten or don't know about, and a couple of long-simmering mystery projects that are still only known by their codenames, Sirius and Hadar.
You'd be forgiven for forgetting about them, given their low profile and drawn-out development times, but in today's H1 investors call , CD Projekt's vice president of investor relations Karolina Gnaś reassured everyone that they're still happening—just not anytime soon.
Asked about Sirius, Gnaś mentioned the recent cuts to the development team , saying—as CD Projekt did when the layoffs happened—that the changes were made to meet "the current needs of the project."
"Pre-production is ongoing, and at this stage we are focused on testing different solutions and ideas we develop," Gnaś said. "This project is very different from our other projects because it's focused on multiplayer. So there's a lot of learning and testing in this particular one."
Sirius first came to light in 2021, when CD Projekt acquired The Molasses Flood , known for The Flame in the Flood , to work on a new game eventually revealed to be based on The Witcher. But the project ran into trouble a couple years later, and was paused and rebooted ; in 2025, CD Projekt's plan to maintain The Molasses Flood as an effectively independent studio also came to an end .
Despite how little we know about Sirius, we know even less about Hadar. It's an all-new property, not based on The Witcher or Cyberpunk, although it will be similar to the extent that it aims to deliver " an emotional, open world experience ." But aside from that? It's " progressing dynamically ," whatever that means, but it's definitely not progressing rapidly: It too has been in the works since 2021 , and Gnaś said it remains "in the concept phase," essentially where it was five years ago.
But it does sound like things might be ready to start picking up speed. "We currently have over 30 people and expect to hire more, up to 50 developers by the end of this year," Gnaś continued. "Right now the team is mostly focused on testing different approaches and ideas, and prototyping some gameplay elements." And then, with an amusing note of finality: "This is it."
Frankly, I'm not too bothered. I am genuinely curious about Hadar, because it's an original thing; Sirius, not so much, because multiplayer's not really my bag and a Witcher game that not all Geralt all the time is fundamentally less interesting to me anyway. But CD Projekt's got enough big stuff cooking I already know about, so if it wants to horse around with these other things until 2033 (or whatever—I have no insights here, 2033 is just suitably far off), that's fine by me.

title: Corsair HS35 v3 review
author: Shaun Prescott
text:
If you skipped buying that coveted stick of RAM or 2 TB SSD this time last year, you must be feeling understandably morose. Most things are getting more and more expensive, but crucially, not all things. Components like headsets and gamepads conform to the fast antiquating dictum that, with time, value will rise while costs decrease.
That's pretty much the case with the Corsair HS35 v3. At the level of raw specs at least, Corsair's new mid-range headset has a touch more to offer than the SteelSeries Arctic Nova 3X, which is our favourite mid-range gaming headset. It came bearing a $90 price tag at launch (though you wouldn't pay full price for it in 2026).
Like the Arctis Nova 3X, the HS35 v3 has 2.4 GHz wireless connectivity, Bluetooth, and a wired option. It has a detachable mic, and reasonably comfortable memory foam ear cups. Both models have 50mm drivers and a 20Hz - 20kHz frequency response. But the HS35 v3 is 10 grams lighter and $10 cheaper. Shots fired!
HS35 v3 specs Style
Over-ear, closed-back
Driver
50 mm with Waves 3D Audio
Frequency response
20 Hz - 20 kHz
Microphone
Omnidirectional
Battery life
Up to 30 hours
Connection
2.4 GHz wireless (Type-C and Type-A dongle), Bluetooth, USB Type-C cable
Weight
250g
Price
$80 | £70 | AU$99
Buy if...
✅ You just want a performant workhorse: The HS35 v3 has excellent audio both incoming and outgoing.
✅ You need something light: This headset is definitely on the lighter end of the spectrum.
Do not buy if...
❌ You want flair: No RGB, few onboard controls, and a pretty boring plastic form factor don't exactly scream "I'm an apex gamer".

Note that's using 2.4 GHz wireless. Mic output quality noticeably deteriorates over Bluetooth, though this is a common issue to do with Bluetooth's narrower bandwidth.
Sonic Assassin
But what I liked most about the HS35 v3 is its remarkable sound, which punches above its weight in this price range. This isn't a noise-cancelling affair but the sonics are nevertheless enveloping, probably thanks in part to the secure embrace of those pivoting earcups. Pummelling theatrical bass leaves plenty of room for the mid-range and all the environmental detail that entails.

I mean, this is not an audiophile set of headphones, nor is it a high range gaming headset, but it handles spiky complexity extraordinarily well, with no clipping or distracting sense of compression.
In Dawnwalker, subterranean dungeons sound genuinely remote and cocooned to a near stifling degree; outside, birds serenely tweet in the foreground as rabid wolves moan in the distance. The HS35 v3 can easily meet the scale of an open world, just as it can capture the cavernous warrens of R6 Siege where audible directional prompts— footsteps, destroyed barricades—are important and not just nice to have.
Sweetness and light
While it performs very well where input and output are concerned, this headset definitely feels mid-range, despite rubbing shoulders with pricier budget affairs. There are some things you'll just have to cope with. Onboard controls are minimal, though we do get a volume wheel which can be pressed to mute the mic, and we do get a single lonely, albeit capable button that can toggle between connectivity modes and pause music. There is no software, which is great news to me, but maybe you like to fiddle with audio profiles.
Battery life is determinedly mid-range as well: expect 30 hours, which does not compare favourably to more expensive models like the HyperX Cloud Alpha Wireless' supernatural 300 hour battery life. But 30 hours is still a long time for anyone but endurance streamers.
The other thing about it is that, well, it's pretty boring. It looks boring and it does what it says it'll do and nothing more. I think this is fine, and I'm not marking it down because it just does the bare minimum, but maybe you like your headsets fancier, in which case: better start saving. For its price, the HS35 v3 does pretty much everything it needs to do with better-than-average performance.

title: Gigabyte GO27Q24A Review
author: Nick Ross
text:
We’ve been reviewing some silly-priced gaming monitors in recent times but, some of the latest-and-greatest models wield premium features that are unnecessary for many buyers. Gigabyte’s GO27Q24A strives to keep things simple by stripping-away some of the less-universally popular, expensive technologies to produce a spartan gaming monitor that focuses on the category’s most-important facets, to keep the price down. Gigabyte has successfully done this before using WOLED and Tandem OLED panels in the same range, so how will this QD-OLED model fare?
Assembling the Gigabyte GO27Q24A is simple: the stem clips to the screen and the stand uses a single thumbscrew to attach to the stem without any tools being needed.
The stand is the same, solid, small-footprint unit that Gigabyte’s premium monitors use and it lets competitive types sit right up close to the screen. The stem is also the same seen on its superior siblings and affords a generous degree of manipulation to get the screen sitting just so: there’s -5°~+21° tilt, ±15° swivel and 90° pivot. There’s also 13 cm of height adjustment. Impressive.
Gigabyte GO27Q24A specs Screen size
27-inch
Resolution
2560 x 1440
Brightness
200 nits fullscreen, 400 nits peak HDR
Response time
0.03 ms
Refresh rate
240 Hz
HDR
DisplayHDR TrueBlack 500
Features
Samsung QD-OLED panel, 2x HDMI 2.1, DisplayPort 1.4, 1x 3.5mm audio jack
Buy if...
✅ You want an affordable, fast QD-OLED gaming monitor: It might not be the brightest, but this fast, colourful, 1,440p display doesn’t put a foot wrong when gaming.
Do not buy if...
❌ You want an all-purpose monitor for work, too: While the screen is usable for office tasks, its glossy finish is prone to reflections and text isn’t the sharpest.
All that comes in the box is a cable-tidy clip that attaches to the stem, and a DisplayPort cable (I rather feel an HDMI cable would be more universally useful). Still, you don’t actually need many cables as there aren’t many places to stick ’em—there are just two HDMI 2.1 ports, a DisplayPort 1.4 port and a headphone jack. Forget your USB-C, KVM hub and optical ports. There’s also no RGB. We’re on a cost-saving mission, here.
Once up and running, you’re presented with a 27-inch, 1440p Windows Desktop that offers plenty of real-estate for work, but displays text that’s a smidge spidery for all-day office use in this day and age—people who often squint at spreadsheets would be better served elsewhere. But, this monitor isn’t for them.
Future Future Future People who often squint at spreadsheets would be better-served elsewhere. But, this monitor isn’t for them.
It’s a Samsung QD-OLED panel (likely Gen 3) which has the usual, impressive-sounding 0.03ms pixel response time and 1:1,500,000 contrast ratio. It also displays 99 percent of the tricky DCI-P3 colour space (so pernickety designer-types will warm to its colour accuracy). However, despite its support for HDR10, the (understated) standout spec is its peak fullscreen brightness of just 200 nits. In a market where everyone (not least Gigabyte) is yelling about their 1,000+ nit brightness, that’s unusually very low (for a QD-OLED panel especially) and likely related to where many of the production costs have been reduced. But, how does it actually perform when gaming?
(Image credit: Future) If you don’t regularly look at super-premium gaming monitors, you could well be wondering where the limitations are. Contrast is excellent, colours are vibrant and, in HDR mode, both colourful and monochromatic transitions and gradients are smooth and step-free. The lack of peak brightness means HDR can be kept active all the time without melting your eyes. It generally does a good job of displaying bright and dark areas of content simultaneously and details still get revealed in darker areas (making it hard for enemies to jump out of shadows) but details can get lost in brighter highlights (not unlike many premium monitors, frankly).
(Image credit: Future) Gigabyte veneers the screen with a semi-gloss, anti-reflective coating which, in some scenarios, does a physics-defeating job at eliminating reflections. However, when viewing dark content, or when you’re in a bright environment, it can still transform into a black mirror.
Nvidia G-Sync and AMD FreeSync Premium technologies are present to help prevent image tearing, and VRR is present to stop brightness flickering. Gigabyte’s also states that its Ultra Clear motion-smoothness technology (black-frame insertion) will be present in a future firmware update, but we’ve heard that one before.
The GO27Q24A also has a fast (0.03 ms stated grey-to-grey) pixel response time and this marries with a 240 Hz refresh rate to keep very-fast-moving objects looking smooth, crisp and clear to the point where only elite-level eSports players might grumble.
(Image credit: Future) Ultimately, it functions very well as a gaming monitor. The HDR peak brightness of 400 nits means the in-your-face, potentially eye-piercing impact of premium models is missing and technical, true-black performance is only very good rather than outstanding (a black screen can feel slightly washed out), but most gamers will care more about the excellent colour vibrancy, contrast and speed on offer.
Future Future Future Gigabyte packs in most of its premium gaming enhancements too. They’re activated by a joystick button at the rear (on the right) of the screen. Their degrees of usefulness will depend on the proclivities of each user and most detrimentally affect overall image quality in some way.
The AI Black Equalizer destroys contrast (to selectable degrees) by brightening dark areas to prevent enemies hiding in very dark shadows. Super Resolution enhances details in areas of uniform colour to make objects look bad but harder to miss.
Night Vision turns the screen green for those who like to LARP as a Navy SEAL super soldier.
Game Info features include adding an on-screen timer that counts up or down. You can add on-screen crosshairs of various designs and offset them from the middle of the screen if necessary. These can be useful when playing CoD in Hardcore mode. Also, unlike (for example) MSI, the crosshair won’t move around the screen every time you move the joystick button.
Night Vision turns the screen green for those who like to LARP as a Navy SEAL super soldier. Flash Dimming helps prevent flashbangs acting like in real-life, while Eagle Eye magnifies the middle of the screen like a sniper scope. I’ve found the latter to be unusably poor in past iterations, but the new implementation (which features a round-shaped ‘optic) feels increasingly like an unfair advantage. Still, it’s still some way off being a hacker tool.
Future Future Future Many of these settings can be activated using Gigabyte’s ‘Tactical Switch’ which sits just below the joystick button. However, the primary function of this is to transform the screen into a more competitive FPS-display. Using the menu, you can change the settings with one press to: 1920 x 1080 (16:9); 1280 x 960 (4:3); 1024 x 768 (4:3); or 1280 x 1024 (5:4) while (potentially) dropping the display-size down to 24 inches. This suits competitive eSports players who sit close to the monitor, want low resolutions for easier headshots and who don’t want to be distracted in their peripheral vision. Clicking the button simply acts like you’ve added a different screen (from Windows’ perspective). It works very well. Unlike other Gigabyte gaming monitors, it doesn’t increase the refresh rate, though.
(Image credit: Future) Another feature that can be activated by the Tactical Switch is pixel cleaning which is part of the OSD’s OLED Care technology. This can automatically (or manually) scan the pixels of your screen and eliminate any dark or bright spots that develop over time. It can also detect static images and logos by arousing the relevant pixels to help prevent burn-in. It works in tandem with Gigabyte’s bespoke, fan-less cooling technology (which uses optimised heat flow channelling, a bespoke heatsink and a graphene film layer) to enhance longevity and back Gigabyte’s three-year warranty that includes burn-in.
(Image credit: Future) At the end of the day, the Gigabyte GO27Q24A doesn’t put a foot wrong. Yes, there are brighter models out there and they might have features like KVM switches and even-faster refresh rates, but these are unnecessary and expensive embellishments to many gamers. The GO27Q24A’s RRP of $450 is low compared to many rivals (and Gigabyte siblings). It even launched at $299 via Newegg for its first month on sale, and we wouldn’t be surprised to see good deals on this again. Frankly, even at $450 it’s a bit of a bargain, but it's hard to look past the excellent Alienware AW2726DM, a monitor that uses the same panel but despite being an Alienware it comes in cheaper.

title: CD Projekt Red isn't 'planning to rely on AI making complete games', and will still be 'predominantly using people' for The Witcher 4 and beyond
author: Harvey Randall
text:
Generative AI in videogame development, despite the looming potentiality of a bubble popping , has continued to be a hot-button topic pelted at developers during earning calls, despite most of them recognising that there's not much use for it beyond mundane busywork.
Sure, it's being used commonly , but rarely for the actual making of the videogame itself. Filling in the roles that procedural generation might or, like, resizing shoulderpads—or for "user preference analysis" . Not exactly the kind of stuff that revolutionises an industry, and certainly not enough to justify reducing labour en masse.
This also seems to be the view of joint CD Projekt Red CEO Michał Nowakowski, who was asked such a question during an earnings conference yesterday, and once more found himself required to emphasise that they're using people to make videogames like The Witcher 4: "AI is definitely becoming a thing in games development as well. We are still predominantly using people and this is our plan—to make games where we're not walking away from that."
That's not to say that AI tools aren't being experimented with , they're just nowhere near a focal or vital part of development for the studio: "AI, if anything, is a tool like many others that's helping in places that can maybe become more helpful in the future but we're not planning to rely on AI making complete games."
Part of that, Nowakowski emphasises, is because the kind of games they make are so complex that it wouldn't make a lick of sense to leave the careful craftsmanship of them up to an LLM or vibe coding: "especially with very complex games like ours, I don't even think this is the right or ethical path to follow.
"So whether this is true for the whole industry, I'm not the person to make those statements. I think everybody has to make those judgments on their own."
Even if you scrap the general distaste for AI slop, it's not like going all-in on the tech is risk free. From a legal standpoint, anti-AI clauses are quickly becoming boilerplate for videogame publishers, at least when it comes to the creative work you'd need to prove you own in a court of law.

Part of that, Nowakowski emphasises, is because the kind of games they make are so complex that it wouldn't make a lick of sense to leave the careful craftsmanship of them up to an LLM or vibe coding: "especially with very complex games like ours, I don't even think this is the right or ethical path to follow.

"So whether this is true for the whole industry, I'm not the person to make those statements. I think everybody has to make those judgments on their own."

Even if you scrap the general distaste for AI slop, it's not like going all-in on the tech is risk free. From a legal standpoint, anti-AI clauses are quickly becoming boilerplate for videogame publishers, at least when it comes to the creative work you'd need to prove you own in a court of law.

title: Dave Bautista is reaching unprecedented levels of buff for his role as Kratos: '2 more months to get to where I need to be'
author: Elie Gould
text:
We got confirmation a few weeks ago that former WWE and Marvel superhero star Dave Bautista would be taking on the role of Kratos in Amazon's upcoming God of War series after an unfortunate accident that saw the previous lead, Ryan Hurst, have to step down from the role after tearing a bicep.
Even before Bautista was confirmed as a replacement, rumours spread of his involvement because, well, he's about one of the only actors who has the physique to step into Kratos' big boots at short notice. But that doesn't even seem enough for the actor, as Bautista has begun an intensive three month long training course.
Dave Bautista shows off his training to play Kratos in the live-action ‘GOD OF WAR’ series.“3rd week in to weight training again. 2 more months to get to where I need to be. Like ridin a bike! LFG!” pic.twitter.com/Oy26Bxs2gZ September 3, 2026
"Third week into weight training again," Bautista writes in an Instagram post . "Two more months to get to where I need to be. Like ridin a bike! LFG!" Given how Bautista looks ready to don the red paint, Leviathan axe, and Blades of Chaos right now, I have no idea what he'll look like after the months of training have come to an end—is there such a thing as too buff for Kratos? Probably not, but we'll see.
But he's not just being used for his muscles. Asad Qizilbash, Sony's head of PlayStation productions and head of product at PlayStation Studios, previously explained how Bautista brings "extraordinary presence, depth, and humanity to the role," in a LinkedIn post . "There's a lot of excitement across PlayStation productions and Santa Monica Studio about what Dave will bring to Kratos, and about continuing to bring this world and these characters to the screen with the care they deserve."
I'm certainly interested to see what Bautista will do with the role of Kratos. I've loved his work in Guardians of the Galaxy, Blade Runner 2049, and Dune Part 2. But I've also always thought that he thrives in oddly comedic roles, and if there's one thing Kratos isn't it's comedic, although that doesn't mean some well-timed and subtle quips are completely off the table.

title: New Final Fantasy 14 site update stabs the final pin into my conspiracy board, leaving me 99.9% sure I know what the new physical ranged job is
author: Harvey Randall
text:
Picture this: I am emerging from a pile of paper, red string, and thumbtacks, hair (I have hair in this scenario) dishevelled, breathless, yelling like I've well and truly lost it: I knew it! I knew we were getting a crossbow in Final Fantasy 14 ! I am then carted away by people in white coats and dispensed in an abandoned warehouse, where Naoki Yoshida emerges with a loaded pistol. I know too much.
Alright, I'm probably not that conspiratorially out of lockstep with the FF14 community about the new job, especially given this latest piece of evidence, but I do feel vindicated. Back during the latest fanfest, some more details emerged about the as-yet-unannounced physical ranged job . Namely, a couple of soundbytes and some trailer snippets.
You can read my full conspiracy board I just linked, which also includes trying to analyse the shape of a catgirl's wand to prove that it was, in fact, a crossbow bolt. And here I am, completely vindicated, because the patch 7.5 site's just been updated with a new image .
Look at what's on her back. That's a crossbow. She's using a crossbow! I knew it! (I proceed to collapse into maniacal, unsettling laughter).
(Image credit: Square Enix) In my mind, this pretty much clinches it: It's almost certain that the physical ranged job in FF14 will be some kind of crossbow-wielding falconer. Square Enix wouldn't just create a new crossbow model (and presumably a ton of bespoke animations) for a job that doesn't exist in-game. Creative Studio 3's a frugal one, sometimes to its own detriment .
Couple this piece of evidence with the soundbytes shared by sound director Masayoshi Soken, the actual Evercold trailer , the job symbol we were shown, the fact we know it's a physical ranged job, that weird lalafell animation glitch—and I admit this is a stretch, but the fact it's a norse themed expansion, and norse mythology loves its birds? I am vindicated. Now and forever.

title: Acer's bizarre hybrid handheld/laptop concept is way more interesting than what is actually getting released this year
author: Jess Kinghorn
text:
While I've bemoaned the expensive state of handheld gaming PCs at length , that doesn't mean I find a cool concept model any less head-turning. Enter Acer's latest Project DualPlay creation: a handheld gaming PC with a flippable screen that can turn into a laptop.
The Project DualPlay Mini was shown off on-stage at IFA 2026, in Berlin . It's all about reimagining "what a gaming handheld form factor can do," exploring a design that functions "both as a gaming handheld and as a mobile productivity station," according to Acer . As a concept machine, however, the Project DualPlay Mini might not see the light of day beyond the IFA stage. What will see a wide release later this year, though, is the Acer Predator Atlas 7.
Very simply, this is a cut-down version of Acer's chunkier Predator Atlas 8 handheld . For starters, the seven-inch touchscreen still enjoys a 120 Hz refresh rate and 500 nits of peak brightness. The device also has an 80Whr battery, and the guts of this new seven-inch form factor still includes Intel Arc B390 graphics, and an Intel Arc G3 Extreme processor. In other words, it's got all of the power, but less of the heft.
It will be available in winter 2026, though the price hasn't yet been announced. For context though, the Predator Atlas 8 ranges in price between $1,300 to $2,000 , and I'm not expecting the Atlas 7 to be priced much differently. With the smaller handheld featuring up to 24 GB LPDDR5x, whatever price is eventually announced will likely be another victim of the raging memory supply crisis .
Even if it could well burn your budget upon release, the Predator Atlas 7's cooling system aims not to burn your fingies too. Like its big sibling, the Atlas 7 enjoys a Predator AeroBlade cooling system, comprising of one plastic fan and one, thinner finned, metal fan (the same system can be found in the Project DualPlay Mini concept machine too). Acer says the metal Predator AeroBlade fan features, "89 blades at just 0.1 mm of thickness" and claims this design delivers an "up to a 10% increase in airflow."
The Acer Predator Atlas 7, a cutdown version of the Atlas 8 handheld gaming PC. (Image credit: Acer) To summarise, the Acer Predator Atlas 7 is 'same, but different.' With handheld pricing being what it is , my excitement is decidedly tempered. The Project DualPlay Mini is definitely cooler, and arguably the brightest idea we've seen from Acer's concept line in a minute (anyone remember this laptop with the pop-out, Joycon-like gamepad ?). But the flippable screen would leave me wondering about the longevity of the device overall, so perhaps it's just as well it's not destined for a store shelf near you.

title: Onimusha on Steam Deck is the definition of 'playable': Surprisingly pleasant, so long as 30 fps isn't a dealbreaker
author: Morgan Park
text:
We're long past the days of assuming the Steam Deck can comfortably handle the new big-budget action game of the moment, but here's a nice surprise: Valve's handheld is not a bad way to play Onimusha: Way of the Sword.
It's not quite the optimization darling that Resident Evil Requiem was earlier this year, but it's much better news than Monster Hunter Wilds or Dragon's Dogma 2. After testing Onimusha in its taxing Kyoto hub area, I'd add this to the win column for Capcom's proprietary engine.
To set expectations: Onimusha is a stubbornly 30-40 fps game on Deck. It can get as high as the 50s and 60s in the right conditions—turning FSR 3.1.4 upscaling on while in corridor areas outside the main hub—but you will eventually shoot back down to the 30s when there's a lot of action on screen. So if you're of the mind that a lower, stable framerate is ultimately the most comfortable way to play a game, then you can confidently lock it at 30 fps and turn off the performance overlay.
That's how I played a decent chunk of it over the last few days, pausing here and there to see which graphical bumps I could get away with. The default configuration cranks everything down to its lowest setting , but I made a few tweaks that meaningfully improve the picture quality without ruining the stable framerate:
Texture quality: Low > Medium
Upscaling: Off
Resolution: 1280 x 800
Frame Rate: 30
Perhaps a few more of the "lows" could become "mediums" without a problem, but truthfully, low already looks pretty good on the Deck's small screen. Capcom has done well not to compromise on the most important part of the picture: Musashi Miyamoto. His model is still nicely detailed, as are the cloth sims of his flowy cloak. That said, upgrading the texture quality to Medium solves the problem of some prominent world objects being noticeably blurry, but that's my only complaint with low preset so far.
Capcom Capcom Capcom Capcom Capcom Capcom Perhaps a controversial choice, but I say turn off Onimusha's FSR 3.1.4 upscaling and take the frames hit. The ghosting effect around moving objects (and especially Musashi's hair) is distracting and ugly, and the gains aren't even that impressive. If 40 is your sweet spot, you'll get it more often with FSR.
I'm only 6 hours into the story, so maybe this changes, but Onimusha isn't so fast-paced that I feel bogged down by the 30 fps lock. Last night I took down the first genuinely challenging boss of the game, Rasho-gan, on the Deck, then switched to my RTX 5090 PC to fight him again. It looked nicer, but I didn't feel a significant advantage.
For my money, Onimusha is the ideal definition of Deck "playable". The performance isn't so impressive that I'd choose to play it handheld when my PC is sitting right there, but it's good enough that I'd happily slice up Genma from the comfort of a hotel room.

title: Onimusha: Way of the Sword has a hard mode, but it isn't unlocked from the start
author: Wes Fenlon
text:
Some players came away from Onimusha's demo worried that the game would be too easy, a concern I've addressed in-depth based on my own time with the game. The good news is that I think the challenge level is well-judged for most people, and Onimusha does have a hard mode.
For those who hoped to jump right into the hardest possible difficulty from the main menu, though, I've got some bad news: you're going to have to beat the game first.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword's default difficulty options
Story : "A difficulty level that lets you focus on the story. Recommended for action game beginners."
Musashi deals more damage and stamina damage and takes less from enemy attacks
Action prompts default to on, showing button icons for how to deal with incoming enemy attacks
Action : "A difficulty level for those who like challenging battles. This difficulty level will keep you on your toes. Recommended for experienced action game players."
You can freely change between these two options from save points throughout the game.
Individually adjustable difficulty tweaks:
Action prompts
Tips (tutorial messages)
Navigation UI icons
(Image credit: Capcom) How to unlock Onimusha: Way of the Sword's Hard mode
There's just one way to unlock Onimusha's harder difficulty level: Finishing the game. No shortcuts, sorry! Here's the in-game description:
Carnage: "A difficulty level where a single hit could mean death. A high-stakes mode where carelessness can kill, but victory is all the sweeter."
If you choose this difficulty, it's locked in. You can't change to Story or Action. But you do get a bit of a leg up, because Carnage is a New Game+ mode that carries over some of your progress from a completed save.
What does the hard mode New Game+ carry over?
Awakened Oni abilities
Enhanced basic and special abilities
Acquired Hozuki Pouches and upgrades
Items, offerings, and "some" materials
Charms and charm upgrades
Unlocked outfits
Tutorial drills and boss rematch unlocks and completion
Genma Notes and rescued Lion Dogs
There's a lot that doesn't carry over to NG+:
Story and sidequest progress
Clothing, sword, and gauntlet upgrades
Materials for those equipment upgrades
Red souls used for upgrades, skill unlocks and buying materials
Spirit Mirror save points
Oni bow
Progression of items buyable with red souls

title: Alien: Isolation 2's Gamescom demo kept its cards close to its chest, but I'm definitely ready to be terrified again
author: Joshua Wolens
text:
It's like seeing an old friend: the clanking in the vents over your head, the way the ribbed tail passes over objects with a thunk-ka-thunk-ka-thunk-ka-thunk , the head-within-a-head, the screaming. You are here, you are back, you have been impaled through the abdomen and killed.
I have played perhaps 20 minutes of Alien: Isolation 2 at Gamescom 2026 and I can tell you this: it is certainly Alien: Isolation. There are some new wrinkles, though—where the first game was a strictly inside affair, stranding you on the space station Sevastopol, the second game sets you down planetside in an entirely new character's shoes. Fewer air vents, fewer vital systems shuddering to a halt; a lot more weather, a lot more space.
You are Blake. Here are the two things to know about Blake: she is not Amanda Ripley—the first game's protagonist who did not feature at all in my time with Alien: Isolation 2—but she is Weyland-Yutani. Specifically, she's Weyland-Yutani management, and isn't that interesting? You're no working class hero. You're now in the shoes of a character who, in any Alien movie worth its salt, would likely reveal themselves as a villain and end up decapitated about 70% of the way through the film.
Planetside, too
The demo Sega and Creative Assembly put together for Gamescom was a little odd. It consisted of (what I must assume are) the game's opening scenes. Blake and a couple of Weyland-Yutani flunkies are on the surface of a planet and checking out a crash site. In practice, this divides the demo into two: the part where you're wandering outside and the bit where you've penetrated the crashed ship.
Why is this weird? Because the crashed ship was, quite literally, an area from the first Alien: Isolation—one of the units Ripley jettisoned from the Sevastopol in her adventures on the cursed station. It's also the only part of the demo that actually featured the xenomorph. That means I never got a chance to experience the alien in the new, outdoor environments, only in one I had already played before.
(Image credit: Sega) I'm happy to predict that being pursued by the xenomorph outside is going to feature whole new dimensions of stress and disorientation over the previous game. In their search for the crash site, Blake and co have to deal with a rising storm on the planet's surface. Rain builds and wind roars, cutting off your senses as you try to navigate the map. I found it stressful, and I wasn't even being chased by a monster at that point.
"You can be in an exterior, and you have the wind and it's really strong, and you throw a flare and it just flies back in your face," says Ana Sopikova, the game's art director, as she describes the new threats you face in the outside world. "What do you do now, right? Or the rain starts and it's really loud and you can't hear the alien's footsteps. So it's basically taken everything that people love, but just adding new layers on top of it… with everything being unscripted, it just creates much more depth in the experience."
Hello, you
After a lot of time getting rained on and lost, I made my way into the crashed ship, and the xenomorph wasted absolutely no time in oozing out of an overhead vent.
All the old fear hormones kicked in. By the end of my time with the first Alien: Isolation, the xenomorph had lost all terror for me. It was just a game mechanic—an obstacle like any other to be circumvented and handled. I guess that immunity wore off, because sneaking about the wreckage of this ship as the alien clanked about over, under, and beside me had my heart rate spiking.
(Image credit: Sega) Creative Assembly's still up to its old tricks. The studio makes ample use of Alien's analogue, mechanical world to force you to zoom in on cranks, valves, computer screens, and save points in ways that kneecap your awareness of the room around you and send your imagination into overdrive. It worked in the first game. It works here.
But it was all quite familiar. Without being able to take the alien outside, my experience of dodging it in the new Isolation felt much like it did in the old one. A lot of throwing objects to distract it, ducking under desks, and fervently praying that it wouldn't turn to walk down the path that would lead it directly to me. All good fun, but I'm ready to see how the xenomorph handles touching grass.
(Image credit: Sega) To hear Creative Assembly tell it, heading planetside will change the game when it comes time for Alien: Isolation 2's release. "In the first game, and in the sequel as well, [the alien] learns and it adapts," says Sopikova. "This is something that we're putting a lot of focus on, because we don't want the player to just pick their favorite tool and keep using it… And obviously, now with more elements, with exteriors, with the weather, with more variables at play, we can really expand on that depth of how the alien learns. What exactly does it learn about you? How does it affect the way it hunts, and how does it affect you ultimately?" Well, I'm eager to find out.

It's like seeing an old friend: the clanking in the vents over your head, the way the ribbed tail passes over objects with a thunk-ka-thunk-ka-thunk-ka-thunk, the head-within-a-head, the screaming. You are here, you are back, you have been impaled through the abdomen and killed.

I have played perhaps 20 minutes of Alien: Isolation 2 at Gamescom 2026 and I can tell you this: it is certainly Alien: Isolation. There are some new wrinkles, though—where the first game was a strictly inside affair, stranding you on the space station Sevastopol, the second game sets you down planetside in an entirely new character's shoes. Fewer air vents, fewer vital systems shuddering to a halt; a lot more weather, a lot more space.

You are Blake. Here are the two things to know about Blake: she is not Amanda Ripley—the first game's protagonist who did not feature at all in my time with Alien: Isolation 2—but she is Weyland-Yutani. Specifically, she's Weyland-Yutani management, and isn't that interesting? You're no working class hero. You're now in the shoes of a character who, in any Alien movie worth its salt, would likely reveal themselves as a villain and end up decapitated about 70% of the way through the film.

Planetside, too

The demo Sega and Creative Assembly put together for Gamescom was a little odd. It consisted of (what I must assume are) the game's opening scenes. Blake and a couple of Weyland-Yutani flunkies are on the surface of a planet and checking out a crash site. In practice, this divides the demo into two: the part where you're wandering outside and the bit where you've penetrated the crashed ship.

Why is this weird? Because the crashed ship was, quite literally, an area from the first Alien: Isolation—one of the units Ripley jettisoned from the Sevastopol in her adventures on the cursed station. It's also the only part of the demo that actually featured the xenomorph. That means I never got a chance to experience the alien in the new, outdoor environments, only in one I had already played before.

I'm happy to predict that being pursued by the xenomorph outside is going to feature whole new dimensions of stress and disorientation over the previous game. In their search for the crash site, Blake and co have to deal with a rising storm on the planet's surface. Rain builds and wind roars, cutting off your senses as you try to navigate the map. I found it stressful, and I wasn't even being chased by a monster at that point.

"You can be in an exterior, and you have the wind and it's really strong, and you throw a flare and it just flies back in your face," says Ana Sopikova, the game's art director, as she describes the new threats you face in the outside world. "What do you do now, right? Or the rain starts and it's really loud and you can't hear the alien's footsteps. So it's basically taken everything that people love, but just adding new layers on top of it… with everything being unscripted, it just creates much more depth in the experience."

Hello, you

After a lot of time getting rained on and lost, I made my way into the crashed ship, and the xenomorph wasted absolutely no time in oozing out of an overhead vent.

All the old fear hormones kicked in. By the end of my time with the first Alien: Isolation, the xenomorph had lost all terror for me. It was just a game mechanic—an obstacle like any other to be circumvented and handled. I guess that immunity wore off, because sneaking about the wreckage of this ship as the alien clanked about over, under, and beside me had my heart rate spiking.

Creative Assembly's still up to its old tricks. The studio makes ample use of Alien's analogue, mechanical world to force you to zoom in on cranks, valves, computer screens, and save points in ways that kneecap your awareness of the room around you and send your imagination into overdrive. It worked in the first game. It works here.

But it was all quite familiar. Without being able to take the alien outside, my experience of dodging it in the new Isolation felt much like it did in the old one. A lot of throwing objects to distract it, ducking under desks, and fervently praying that it wouldn't turn to walk down the path that would lead it directly to me. All good fun, but I'm ready to see how the xenomorph handles touching grass.

To hear Creative Assembly tell it, heading planetside will change the game when it comes time for Alien: Isolation 2's release. "In the first game, and in the sequel as well, [the alien] learns and it adapts," says Sopikova. "This is something that we're putting a lot of focus on, because we don't want the player to just pick their favorite tool and keep using it… And obviously, now with more elements, with exteriors, with the weather, with more variables at play, we can really expand on that depth of how the alien learns. What exactly does it learn about you? How does it affect the way it hunts, and how does it affect you ultimately?" Well, I'm eager to find out.

title: Guild Wars 3's approach to combat and movement is like nothing I've ever seen in an MMO before: 'One of our big goals when we make a new game in the Guild Wars franchise is to set out and try new things'
author: Fraser Brown
text:
There are few things as exciting as the prospect of a new MMO. And when that new MMO is from ArenaNet, the studio that's been focused on Guild Wars for more than two decades, the excitement is even greater. Having seen Guild Wars 3 in action at Gamescom, and spoken to game director Colin Johanson and lead combat designer Kevin Stocker, my excitement has been justified.
Just as Guild Wars 2 was dramatically different from its predecessor, Guild Wars 3 is not a simple sequel. It's distinct from GW2, a very different kind of MMO, and one that even in the short space of time I spent watching it being played is full of novel ideas.
(Image credit: ArenaNet) The first big change is in its setting. The clock has been turned back 1,000 years, and we're heading to Orr—a land that in GW2's era is a post-apocalyptic hellscape, but at this earlier point is a verdant wilderness teeming with spirits.
"The origins of the Guild Wars franchise originate out of Orr," says Johanson. "This is a time before the gods have left the world, very shortly after Grenth has usurped Dhuum and become the god of death. This is a time where the first guilds are starting to rise across the world, and before the very first Guild War takes place. And there is 21 years of Guild Wars history, and so much of it originates out of this timeline and this setting."
As someone who's been playing Guild Wars since I was still in university, a trip back in time to see what led up to all the events I've played through is a compelling prospect. So the choice in setting offers a lot to veterans, but ArenaNet also picked this era because it's a great starting point for new players. You don't need any foreknowledge, because nothing that happened in the previous games has come to pass in Guild Wars 3. We're all going in pretty fresh.
The joy of movement
(Image credit: Arenanet) The focus of this first hands-off demo is movement and combat, and it doesn't disappoint. Stocker takes control of a Warrior as Johanson talks me through what's happening. The Warrior jumps off a cliff, and immediately brings out her glider—a familiar mode of transport for Guild Wars 2 players. But then something new happens. Stocker spots some creatures below, so he attacks them from above, seamlessly swapping from gliding to a drop attack. This is all part of the new momentum system, and it's awesome.
One of our big goals when we make a new game in the Guild Wars franchise is to set out and try new things.
Colin Johanson
"One of our big goals when we make a new game in the Guild Wars franchise is to set out and try new things, and to innovate and to push the genre forward," says Johanson. Early on, the team identified movement as one of the places where it could shake MMOs up, building on the work it did in Guild Wars 2 with gliding, jumping puzzles and mounts.
"One of the things that you constantly see [in MMOs] is that there's this really stop-start nature to movement," he continues. "You're running, then you stop and then you jump, then you stop and then you glide. Everything feels very clunky."
(Image credit: ArenaNet) ArenaNet wanted to evoke action games, where there's no stopping and starting, just seamless switching between different styles of movement. Thus momentum became a "core component" to Guild Wars 3. The result is that there's now mantling, wall running, gliding in all directions, and your speed actually matters. The faster you're moving, the more force you're building up. This is how it affects combat.
"It ended up being a really natural development to bring the two systems together," Stocker tells me. "As soon as we got to the point where you could wall run into this leap and slam sequence, it was a huge hit in the studio, and so we took a step back and went through all of the combat—we're going for a much more visceral kind of action combat—and did a bunch of work to tie everything together. So everything you're doing in movement, whether it's dashing or wall running or gliding, seamlessly goes into your combat skills and actually pays off."
So the more momentum you have, the greater the impact you make when you're attacking. Doing a drop attack from a great height increases both the damage of your attack and the radius.
Knockabout
(Image credit: ArenaNet) This ties nicely into combat's increased physicality. You can knock enemies around—and be knocked around yourself—netting you extra damage. Kicking a monster into a wall will do more damage than just kicking it. And you can knock enemies off cliffs, doing even more damage, or killing them outright. Guild Wars 3 also takes into account the size of your opponent. So you'll need more momentum to knock back larger enemies.
Even in a hands-off demo, it was clear how different this is going to feel compared to other MMOs. Knockbacks are a common tool in countless MMO arsenals, sure, but they are usually designed to stun or to give players breathing room. And on the rare occasion when you can knock an enemy off a ledge, like in Star Wars: The Old Republic, it often breaks the encounter. It's usually far from a combat pillar.
Guild Wars 3's classes also feature different skills that enhance these abilities—basically multiplayer combos. When Johanson and Stocker teamed up to explore a ruined temple, Johanson was able to use Stocker's shield as a springboard, increasing their momentum and allowing them to get behind the enemy to target a weak point.
(Image credit: ArenaNet) While I didn't see the Ranger class, Stocker tells me it has a particularly cool ability that creates a vortex that sends all their allies up into the air, where they can comfortably pull off their aerial attacks.
Customising your build and bringing the right skills to defeat enemies is another huge part of combat.
Colin Johanson
We eventually get to my least favourite part of MMOs and RPGs: the spider section. Stocker is taking his warrior through an arachnid-infested den that's covered in sticky webs. My phobia flares up. "These are really difficult to kill," says Johanson. "It takes a long time because of their webs." Their webs can target players, slowing down both attacks and movement, but they can also spread across the ground, affecting everyone in the area.
But there's good news for my fellow arachnophobes—they can be handled deftly with the right build. "Customising your build and bringing the right skills to defeat enemies is another huge part of combat," says Johanson. And conveniently, Stocker has an ability that modifies his attacks, and those of his allies, by adding fire damage. This tears through webs, so you can quickly set your allies free. Spiders are particularly weak to fire damage, too, so they go down rapidly.
Feed your spirit
(Image credit: ArenaNet) Earlier I mentioned that Orr is teeming with nature spirits. They weren't the focus of this first demo, but I did get ArenaNet to share a little bit about what role they'll play. Because the gods haven't yet seen fit to share magic with mortals—despite the region being rife with it—the denizens of Orr have needed to find other ways to take advantage of it. The Vaelwardens have access to crafted signets that give them access to magic, but much of the magic in Guild Wars 3 comes from befriending spirits.
Back in the ruined temple, Stocker uses a spirit to illuminate the darkness. "You can actually befriend it and eventually summon it so that you can see in dark places," says Johanson. And your mounts, both flying and ground-based, will be spirits as well, which you'll need to befriend before you can take advantage of their movement capabilities.
Your enemies can use spirits as well. We meet a fire-spewing foe in the temple who has captured a spirit and stuck it in a backpack—this is what's fuelling their fire attacks. What's cool, though, is this makes them vulnerable. So you can use momentum to get behind them, damage the backpack, free the spirit, and then easily take out the defanged enemy.
(Image credit: Arenanet) In a relatively short space of time I got to see so many things that Guild Wars 3 is doing differently, and it's properly exciting to see an upcoming MMO that isn't content with just doing the same thing over and over again, or trying to drum up nostalgia for old sandbox MMOs. Guild Wars 3 seems to be confidently charting its own course—which in turn has given me a lot more confidence in its ability to have some real staying power.
Of course, there's still a lot of questions. How is it handling PvP, for instance? PvP has always been central to the series, so expectations are high. Magic, spirits, mounts, dungeons, character progression, character customisation—there's a lot to dig into between now and its beta, due in autumn 2027.

title: PUBG's new spin-off game is 'faster, meaner, and more aggressive' with sword hands and 'a little bit of light cannibalism'
author: Mollie Taylor
text:
PUBG remains one of Steam's most-played games, which makes it all the more surprising that PUBG Studios and publisher Krafton haven't made more attempts to milk it over the years. PUBG: DED NET might be the biggest yank of the udder to date though, revealing an entirely new spin-off roguelite FPS set in the '90s. And if you didn't know the game was set in the '90s, you sure will after the game's trailer beats you over the head with period-accurate vibes.
Creative director Dave Curd helpfully informs me that the "DED" in DED NET stands for "dog eat dog," which makes the words emblazoned across one of the miniguns in the trailer make a whole lot more sense. I've sat down with Curd in the hours after the game's reveal at Gamescom's Opening Night Live, where he tells me a little bit more about what players can expect from DED NET.
Curd says DED NET is going to be "unhinged" and "unfiltered" with the promise of tons of build variety that'll unfurl the more matches you play. "Every run starts different, and you'll always have something in mind. Maybe this run I want to be the very close quartered, door kicker, riot shield guy. Maybe this run I want to be more of a trickster or prankster, and I'm going to hack payphones and play dead, and maybe indulge in a little bit of light cannibalism. But between each match, you're always kind of going with the flow of the game over the multi-match journey."
It's not just guns and trickery that'll pave the way to victory. There's also, y'know, sword hands. "One of the themes is sacrificing flesh for power," Curd tells me. "So losing the ability to manipulate guns or even drive. You can jump in the passenger seat, but you can't drive the car anymore when you've got the blade hands. But you're absolutely hellacious in melee distance."
Curd says it's "just one of the 70-plus abilities and changes" that you'll be able to tinker around with in DED NET, with its roguelite elements meaning "the more you play, the more control, the more engagement, the more connection you have with your journey."
(Image credit: Krafton) As for why DED NET isn't just a mode in the OG PUBG: Battlegrounds? "The two things that made this deserve to be its own thing are the pace and persistence. Our map is smaller, it's denser, it's more intense. The movement, the player behaviours and player mechanics are more aggressive and athletic. PUBG is deliberate and thoughtful and tactical. This is not that. The tactics are there in terms of your build crafting and theorycrafting … if I'm a PUBG fan booting this up for the first time it's going to be faster, meaner, and more aggressive than I'm used to."
All of this is to the backdrop of some intensely '90s vibes, which Curd tells me was a hugely formative era for him. "It's such an interesting historical tension point," he said. "One foot in the analogue world, one foot in the digital world. You didn't have a cell phone on you at all times. You had to use payphones. The guns were cool. Live-streamed music was finally happening. You also saw the birth of really exploitative reality TV and blood sport like EWC or UFC cage fighting."
(Image credit: Krafton) Taking that grungey, lesser-connected time and bringing it to life in DED NET doesn't just stop at its visuals—it's bringing music from that era to the forefront as well. "We have very fleshed out grunge and hip-hop stations," Curd tells me. "You'll hear stuff from Toadies, Nine Inch Nails, Local H. We have Biggie [Smalls], we have Ice Cube. It's a really fun soundtrack."
Curd's enthusiasm for DED NET isn't to be underestimated. Though for those of us without a peek behind the curtain right now and only a cinematic trailer to go off, a double dip into the PUBG universe might be a harder sell for those who are still deeply attached to the original.
If the idea of a chaotic all-American '90s gunfest has got you all giddy though, you can register for a chance to hit up PUBG: DED NET's closed beta test which should be arriving some time in the near future.

title: Final Fantasy 7 Revelation gets a release date and a proper look at its airship overworld, which is cool, if in danger of inducing open world fatigue
author: Harvey Randall
text:
If there's one thing that's become daunting about the modern RPG, it's the ballooning time investment. There's no better example than the Final Fantasy 7 Remake trilogy, a reimagining of a classic that has stretched itself out between three entire fully-fledged games.
Final Fantasy 7 Revelation just had its release date dropped alongside a 10-minute gameplay deep dive during PlayStation's State of Play . In it, we got to see a closer look at the airship overworld.
It's pretty dang impressive. Your airship'll let you zip around the open world in record time, showing you a charming mini-model of each zone—it's not one hundred percent seamless (there's a cutscene between choosing a landing spot and parachuting down that's doubtless there to disguise some loading) but the ability to parachute down anywhere is neat, and it feels like a modern-day realisation of what the classic airship overworld of older RPGs were trying to do.
We saw this in practice in a couple of locations, including Wutai—wherein Yuffie was able to grapple hook to a nearby roof and have a roam around. And yet, despite how impressive this all looks, I can't help but feel a certain dread set in.
I haven't played FF7 Rebirth yet, just Remake—owing partially to a lack of spare hours to pour into it on my part, but also a resistance to the idea of playing what my co-workers have told me is a great big stonking open world. To settle down and follow that shot up with the chaser of yet another massive, expansive open world just to round out a trilogy is enough to make me want to sleep for a thousand years.
Assuming a similar playtime to completion as its past two games, and assuming you don't do everything these games have to offer, that'll be a stonking 150-odd hours to round out the entire trilogy—quite literally tripling the game it was originally remaking. title: Crimson Desert's upcoming DLC decides it's The Sims now, I guess
author: Mollie Taylor
text:
Crimson Desert is like the videogame version of a 6-in-1 shampoo—it does just about everything, and with its upcoming DLC Charting the Unknown, I guess that also includes The Sims.
Today's State of Play showed off a trailer with what we can expect to see, and there's a lot. Like building a whole-ass castle, for example. It looks like you can go pretty ham on some Sims-style building within those stony walls, too—the trailer shows a tool which you can drag to build walls and rooms inside the castle. Yup, just like The Sims! There's a whole bunch of furniture as well, including a slightly unusual framed portrait of a tiger that Kliff has deigned to display outside his home, for whatever reason.
It looks like you'll be able to build a village around this castle as well, perhaps similar to the Greymanes camp you form in the main game. There are people cooking, little village stalls, and plenty of chatter that seems to be happening either within the castle walls or just outside of them. How different it'll be to the Greymane's camp remains to be seen, but it is looking like a surprisingly cosy endeavour.
Something I am curious about, though, is the fact it looks like Kliff can romance (or at least gussy up to) other characters. There's a tiny snippet of him offering flowers to one of the game's witches—something she seems pretty darn jazzed about, by the way—though it's unclear what purpose it actually serves. I wonder how Kliff would actually rizz anyone in Crimson Desert, for how limited his dialogue is.
Some other bits I noticed include:
Running on water
Underwater traversal, including grabbing onto a shark like some sort of aquatic Uber
Both a traditional looking ship and something more steampunk-looking
Fellow Greymane Andrew cheffing it up in the castle
Some crazy laser-eyed mechanical cyclops monster
The most surprising part of all of this, though? Charting the Unknown is set to release October 15. Yes, this October. A mere seven months after launching and somehow cooked up in the midst of a dizzying number of patches and tweaks that have contorted Crimson Desert into something that is completely unlike the game I reviewed back in March.
How Pearl Abyss has managed to do all of this is beyond me, but hey, it's coming pretty darn soon. I am admittedly pretty giddy at the idea of going full Sims-esque castle building, so I'll undoubtedly be returning to Pywel before long.

title: Both Microsoft and Sony say they're under no obligation to pass tariff refunds on to customers
author: Jess Kinghorn
text:
Tech tariffs imposed by the Trump administration were ruled unconstitutional back in February , though the saga is far from over. Many companies have since sought refunds, and consumers battling rising hardware prices are wondering whether they'll see those recouped costs trickle down. Well, as far as major players Microsoft and Sony are concerned, the answer is 'No.'
To rewind a smidge, consoles have been climbing in price for some time now. An Xbox gamer filed a proposed class-action lawsuit against Microsoft back in July , accusing the company of passing on the cost of tariffs to consumers. A similar lawsuit was filed against Sony back in May . Now, lawyers from both companies are arguing that their respective sides are simply under no obligation to pass on tariff refunds to customers.
As reported by Game File , Microsoft’s legal team filed a motion to dismiss its lawsuit last month, saying, "There is nothing unjust about Plaintiff purchasing an Xbox at an advertised price and getting exactly what he paid for—regardless of whatever theory he devised months later about Microsoft’s cost structure."
Sony's lawyers reportedly filed their motion to dismiss on Monday, arguing, "Paying fair market price for voluntarily purchased consumer goods is not a legally cognizable injury in fact."
Sony had previously estimated it would see $508 million in tariff refunds , with the company's chief financial officer reportedly having since said that "most" of this would be recouped by the gaming division. The fact that consumers won't directly see any of that feels unfair, but it is perhaps unsurprising.
(Image credit: Nintendo) Nintendo has also sought tariff refunds and similarly saw a consumer lawsuit filed against it back in April. PC Mag reported that Nintendo's lawyers filed a motion to dismiss in July. Their filing says , "Plaintiffs ask this Court to invent a legal duty out of whole cloth to retroactively re-price completed sales simply because the legal landscape has changed."
Nintendo's lawyers went on to add, "Taken to its logical extension, Plaintiffs’ theory would require every business that raises a price to recompute its prices and repay consumers if some pricing assumption proves mistaken."
But not all hardware companies are following suit. For one thing, Arctic announced a price rollback after securing its refund, saying this will continue until " every single dollar Arctic received [...] has been paid back to our customers ."
Panic, maker of the Playdate handheld, has taken a bolder stance, offering refunds to those who bought its console and were charged extra for its tariffs. Company co-founder Cabel Sasser said last month, " It's just not our money to keep ."
If only more gaming and hardware companies agreed.

title: Stalker 2 studio is raffling keychains made from a shot-down Russian helicopter to raise funds for mine removal in the real-world Chornobyl Exclusion Zone
author: Andy Chalk
text:
Stalker 2 studio GSC Game World has joined with Ukrainian charity United24 on a new fundraising initiative that aims to raise $100,000 to help fund efforts to remove mines and other explosive devices from the real-world Chornobyl Exclusion Zone.
The Zone—the real one—was established in 1986 following the disaster at the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant. It's not quite as fanciful as the videogame counterpart but it is hazardous, and public access is restricted; as one of the most radioactively contaminated regions on the planet, it's also of considerable scientific interest.
Facilities in the zone also require ongoing maintenance, which became a problem when Russian troops seized the Zone and power plant during the early days of the invasion of Ukraine. The troops withdrew a couple months later—some reportedly received "significant doses" of radiation during their time there—leaving behind mines and explosives that pose a significant hazard to returning workers and researchers: United24 says at least eight explosions have wounded or killed staff and soldiers since the Russian withdrawal.
"Demining the Chornobyl Exclusion Zone is first and foremost about the safety of the people who work there every day—scientists and energy workers," said Ihor Bezkaravainyi of Ukraine’s Ministry of Economy and Environment. "Particular attention is being paid to creating safe routes for firefighting and rescue teams, allowing them to respond to fires in the Zone more quickly, without putting their lives at risk from mines."
Clearing mines is its own reward—the United Nations reported in 2025 that civilian injuries and deaths caused by landmines had reached their highest level in four years , in part due to funding shortfalls for demining efforts—but anyone who kicks in a minimum of $10 to GSC's fundraising campaign will have a shot at some swag, including patches, t-shirts, Stalker 2: Heart of Chornobyl Ultimate Edition keys, and a pretty groovy collectible statuette.
The real pièce de résistance , though, are the five "Artifact keychains" carved out of the wreckage of a Russian Mi-8 helicopter that was shot down over the Zone. Sweet.
(Image credit: GSC Game World/United 24) "Chornobyl is the beating heart of our gaming universe," GSC Game World said. "For us, it’s far more than just a setting or a narrative backdrop—it’s a vital piece of the Ukrainian cultural code and an inseparable part of our identity. Today, amid the ongoing war, we want our work to carry real-world power and help our country overcome the devastating consequences of the Russian invasion.
"That is why this new joint project to demine the Exclusion Zone is a deeply symbolic and meaningful mission for our entire studio. Having had a fantastic experience collaborating with United24 in the past, we are immensely proud to continue this partnership. Our goal is simple: ensure that danger exists only within the game, while real Ukrainian soil becomes safe once again as quickly as possible."
GSC Game World's first collaboration with United24 raised more than $120,000 for the Bring Light Back campaign to provide generators for schools in Ukraine, which suffers from frequent power failures and blackouts as a result of the ongoing war. Donations to GSC's demining campaign can be made at u24.gov.ua .

title: Zach Cregger doesn't want to get bogged down in 'the wild aspects' of Resident Evil's lore: 'I'm not going to have a gigantic jacked dude in a trench coat'
author: Elie Gould
text:
What's the weirdest bit of Resident Evil lore you know of? Is it the fact that Claire Redfield's favourite food is a cheeseburger? Maybe it's that Hunk spent a week lost in Raccoon City's sewers eating rats after getting his ass beaten by Birkin? Or perhaps it's that the Tyrant's trench coat is more than just a bold fashion statement—it's actually integral to the build.
There's been a few explanations as to why Tyrants wear trench coats in Resident Evil games. One perk of the coat is that it helps disguise the mutations, which allows Tyrants to infiltrate more sensitive areas, but its biggest bonus is its power-limiting function. Wearing the trench coat holds the Tyrant together by preventing out-of-control mutations, and if it's damaged or the Tyrant removes it you'll get a Super Tyrant.
(Image credit: Capcom) You'd be forgiven for not knowing this as it's not exactly a widely talked about tidbit, which is exactly why Zach Cregger, director of the upcoming Resident Evil movie, is staying away from Resident Evil's deep lore: to keep the film as grounded as possible.
"Some of the Resident Evil games get a little magical," Cregger says during a recent junket (via DiscussingFilm ). "You know we have a woman who can turn into birds [he means Mother Miranda] and fly around. I love it, I love it, I've played [Resident Evil 8] a bunch of times, I think it's an awesome game, but in terms of me making a movie out of it, it's like I gotta try and limit some of the wild aspects of Resident Evil.
Zach Cregger says he chose to keep his ‘RESIDENT EVIL’ movie as grounded as possible.“I’m not gonna have a gigantic jacked dude in a trench coat because I’m like ‘where did the coat come from?’… the T-Virus does all sorts of cool mutations that's enough.” pic.twitter.com/Opw4yoJ2sH September 3, 2026
"So I chose to stick with the T-virus, keep it as grounded as possible. So that means I'm not going to have a gigantic jacked dude in a trench coat, because I'm like, 'Where'd the coat come from? How did he get the coat?'"
The was, expectedly, met with a flurry of fury as some accused Cregger of not understanding the intricacies of Resident Evil. But they've failed to see that Cregger actually does understand "why [the Tyrant] exists and why he has the coat". It's not that Cregger doesn't know about the structural integrity of the trench coat, it's just that he doesn't believe it's valuable information for a film, and he's right.
The T-virus has all kinds of cool and fun mutations—that is enough.
Zach Cregger
There's so much to Resident Evil that it's completely unrealistic to think that anyone could condense it all down into a manageable chunk for a film which will likely be under two hours long. It also has to appeal to more than just fans of the game: Someone who has never heard of Resident Evil should be able to watch this film and have a good time without getting confused or bogged down in excessive lore and fan service. Striking that balance is truly an artform.
Kane Parsons actually managed to pull this off with his Backrooms movie. For those who were knowledgeable about Backrooms the film was full of references and easter eggs, like Clarks furniture store being a reference the photo that inspired the Backrooms as well as other small info dumps about Parsons' Backrooms YouTube series. But you didn't need any prior knowledge to enjoy the film, which is what I think Cregger is gunning for with Resident Evil.
"In the world of this [film] where the outbreak just happened, I want to keep it chaotic, I want to keep it primal, and I want to just keep it just as grounded as I can," Cregger says. "The T-virus has all kinds of cool and fun mutations—that is enough. So I'm limiting it there."
